topics.title: Chapter 54 — Measuring Performance
topics.summary: Performance engineering begins by defining the work and the measurement boundary. A number is meaningful only when it identifies what completed, under which conditions, and how the observation was made. Correctness checks belong in the experiment: a program that skips work can appear extraordinarily fast. This chapter distinguishes measured observations , analytical models , and illustrative assumptions . The companion benchmark reports local timings when run, but the book does not convert one container run into a universal hardware claim. Reproduce measurements on the machine and workload that matter. [ R30 , R42 ]

topics.title: 54.1 Latency
topics.summary: Latency measures elapsed time from a defined start event to a defined completion event. For a request, the boundary might include queueing, parsing, computation, and response delivery. For a kernel, it might include only the computation after inputs are prepared. Report a distribution when requests vary. A mean can hide a long tail, and a percentile requires enough samples and a clearly defined population. Do not compare one system’s median service time with another system’s end-to-end 99th percentile as though they were the same metric.

topics.title: 54.2 Throughput
topics.summary: Throughput measures completed useful work per unit time. It can be expressed as records, requests, or bytes per second. Define whether failed requests, retries, warmup work, and partial completions count. Throughput and latency interact through queueing. A system can increase completed work by admitting more concurrent requests while making each request wait longer. Evaluate the service objective rather than maximizing a single number without constraints.

topics.title: 54.3 CPU time
topics.summary: CPU time measures processor execution charged to a process or thread under the operating system’s accounting rules. It excludes many periods spent blocked or not scheduled. A multithreaded process can accumulate more total CPU time than elapsed wall time when several threads execute concurrently. CPU time helps distinguish computation from waiting, but it is not a complete explanation. Kernel activity, helper processes, and accounting boundaries may contribute differently. State whether the measurement covers one thread, the whole process, or a larger job.

topics.title: 54.4 Wall-clock time
topics.summary: Wall-clock elapsed time includes waiting, scheduling delays, and other activity between the chosen start and end. For duration measurements, use a monotonic clock such as std::chrono::steady_clock rather than a civil-time clock that can be adjusted. Clock resolution and call overhead matter for very small operations. Batch enough work to make the measured interval meaningful, while ensuring that the batch still represents the workload and does not change cache behavior beyond the intended experiment.

topics.title: 54.5 Utilization
topics.summary: Utilization describes the fraction of a resource’s capacity in use under a stated definition. CPU utilization, memory bandwidth utilization, and device busy time are different metrics. High CPU utilization does not prove that useful work is progressing efficiently; a spin loop can consume an entire core. Low utilization does not automatically mean spare end-to-end capacity. The bottleneck may be a serialized dependency, a lock, a downstream service, or a limit in another resource. Identify the constrained stage before adding more work.

topics.title: 54.6 Benchmarking
topics.summary: A benchmark should state input size and distribution, build configuration, machine context, warmup policy, repetition count, and correctness criteria. Keep setup outside the timed region when the goal excludes setup, and include it when evaluating end-to-end behavior. Preserve observable results so the compiler cannot legally discard the intended work as unused. Inspect generated code when a result seems implausible. Avoid volatile as a blanket benchmarking technique because it can change the workload being measured rather than merely prevent elimination.

topics.title: Worked example — A checksum-protected timing boundary
topics.summary: This program constructs a bounded runtime-sized vector, times one summation, and verifies the sum against an independent formula. Setup and verification are outside the timed interval. The output timing is an observation on the machine where it is run, not a fixed expected value. Companion listing: ch54/benchmark.cpp For count 1000, there are three complete groups of values 0 through 250 and a remainder of 247 values, 0 through 246. The expected sum is 3 × 31375 + 247 × 246/2 = 124506 . The elapsed nanoseconds vary. A zero or very small reported duration for a tiny input can reflect clock granularity or overhead dominance rather than infinite throughput. The program is a measurement-mechanics example, not a complete microbenchmark framework. Repeat separate runs, record build flags, inspect the loop, and compare like conditions before interpreting a performance difference. Allocation failure is reported by the C++ runtime unless a surrounding application adds a more specific recovery policy.
